business: RAM Law (Rebenack Aronow & Mascolo LLP), New Brunswick NJ, with offices in Somerville and Manalapan
opportunity: After-hours and overflow bilingual telephone intake agent: answer, structure the intake, flag deadlines and duplicates, route by office, book callbacks, and hand injuries to on-call staff while lawyers keep every acceptance decision (audit opportunity #1)

problem.summary: RAM Law advertises 'Phone Intake Hours 24/7' at intake while its published office hours are Monday-Friday 8:00 AM-8:00 PM with Saturday and Sunday closed, so every call after 8pm or on a weekend is handled by someone other than office staff - most likely an outside answering or intake service, which is an inference, since the firm never says who picks up. The firm publishes only two intake channels, a phone number and a web form, with one shared mailbox (contact@ram.law) for all three offices and no scheduling calendar, portal or status lookup. Because the firm works on contingency, a first contact that is answered badly, described to a stranger, or re-keyed the next morning is directly revenue-relevant, and the re-keying falls on paralegals whose roles are the only support roles the firm names. The site already carries call tracking, a legal intake widget and a purchased-lead tag, so leads arrive from several directions and all have to be reconciled into one intake record.

solution.design: Do not replace anything the firm already pays for. Keep Lawbrokr as the website intake surface, keep Gravity Forms as the form, keep CallRail as the attribution layer, and add one missing layer: a bilingual voice-and-form agent that owns the after-hours and overflow window. Inbound calls to the firm's published number are forwarded (after hours, or when the front desk does not pick up within N rings) to a dedicated Telnyx number attached to a Telnyx Voice AI agent; after-hours form submissions hit the same agent through a Gravity Forms webhook. On every contact the agent: (1) states a recording/AI-assistant disclosure and offers Spanish; (2) collects a fixed intake schema - incident date, county and location, injury and treatment status, whether police responded, whether a commercial truck or public entity is involved, insurance/UM-UIM posture, other driver's carrier, language preference, best callback window; (3) computes a conservative deadline flag from the incident date (2-year personal-injury limitation, and a hard 'check public-entity notice' flag whenever a government body might be involved) and never states a deadline to the caller as advice; (4) checks for duplicates against the last 12 months of intakes and runs a name/party conflict screen against existing matters and adverse parties; (5) routes by county to New Brunswick, Somerville or Manalapan and by practice area, then books a named callback slot in the shared calendar and sends one SMS plus one email confirmation; (6) for out-of-scope or clearly non-qualifying contacts, drafts a decline/referral note for a human to approve rather than refusing on the call. Escalation: any call describing an active injury, an unrepresented hospitalised person, a tow-truck or insurer pressure, an imminent court date, or a caller who asks for a lawyer is warm-transferred to the on-call rotation within seconds; any call the agent scores low-confidence is queued for a human callback and flagged as 'do not answer' to the caller. Human gates: the agent never accepts or declines a case, never discusses fees, liens or case value, never says 'we will represent you', and never sends an outbound message on a matter without a human click during the pilot. Logging: audio, transcript, structured JSON, confidence scores, escalation reason and reviewer ID are written to an append-only per-intake record that the COO can export for a supervision file, with audio retention configurable (default 90 days) and no model training on firm or caller data. Deployment is Telnyx-hosted voice runtime in a single tenant with zero-retention settings on the language model, rather than a per-seat SaaS chatbot, because privileged caller narratives cannot be handled by an anonymous consumer endpoint under NJ's AI guidance.

solution.human_in_the_loop: Three hard gates. (1) Legal judgement stays human: case acceptance, declination, fee and lien discussion, and anything that could create an attorney-client relationship are drafted or flagged by the agent and decided by a lawyer or the COO. (2) Every outbound message during the pilot is approved by a person before it leaves; after the pilot, only templated callback confirmations send automatically. (3) Hot-injury and deadline calls bypass the agent entirely by warm transfer to the on-call rotation. A named supervising attorney signs a written runbook that lists exactly what the agent may say, the escalation triggers, the prohibited phrases (no advice, no dollar figures, no deadline statements), and the weekly review of a sample of transcripts - which is what RPC 5.3 supervision of a nonlawyer (or automated) assistant requires in practice.

pilot.scope: After-hours (8pm-8am), weekend and daytime-overflow inbound calls plus after-hours web form submissions only. Bilingual. Structured intake record and duplicate/conflict flag for every contact; callback slots booked; hot-injury warm transfer to the on-call rotation; daily reconciliation of CallRail/Juvo leads against created intakes. Explicitly out of scope: weekday live call handling, case acceptance, fee discussion, trust accounting, records chasing and any client-status messaging.
pilot.weeks: 3-4 weeks live after a 3-4 week build (7-8 weeks from signed agreement)
success_metrics: After-hours contacts captured (answered + structured record created) vs the pre-pilot baseline of after-hours calls answered/abandoned
Median time from contact to booked callback slot (target: booked during the call)
Structured-record completeness: share of contacts with all required fields filled (target 90%+)
Field accuracy on blind-reviewed sample: critical-field error rate under 5% (incident date, county, injury status, phone number)
Escalation quality: 100% of simulated hot-injury calls transferred within 60 seconds; zero calls where the agent accepted a case, quoted a fee or stated a deadline
Spanish parity: share of Spanish-language calls completed without a language-based transfer
Zero confirmed cross-caller data exposure and zero unapproved outbound messages
Staff time per intake (timed on a sample) vs the pre-pilot manual baseline
pilot.baseline_method: Two months of the firm's own CallRail after-hours data (calls offered, answered, missed, voicemail, duration) plus a timed observation of 15 real intakes during week 1, both recorded in a one-page baseline memo signed by the COO before go-live. Nothing is compared to an industry benchmark, because no peer-reviewed measurement of law-firm intake savings was located.
pilot.exit_criteria: Pilot converts only if all of the following hold: after-hours capture is at or above baseline; critical-field error rate is under 5% on the final blind review; no unresolved confidentiality or supervision finding; the runbook's prohibited-phrase test passes on 50 consecutive calls; and the COO and supervising attorney both sign the monthly scope. If any fails, the founder hands back the runbook, transcripts and a written findings memo, and the pilot ends with no monthly fee.

suggested_pricing.pilot_fee: $1,500 fixed for the 3-4 week live pilot (after-hours + overflow only, up to 2,000 voice minutes), invoiced 50% at kickoff and 50% at go-live - INFERENCE
suggested_pricing.setup_fee: $3,500 one-time on conversion, covering intake-schema build, case-management write-back, Spanish QA, the attorney-signed runbook, staff training and the baseline/exit reporting pack - INFERENCE
suggested_pricing.monthly_fee: $650/month for the after-hours and overflow scope with up to 2,000 voice minutes, then $0.10/minute overage; 12-month term, 30 days' notice; daytime live-call handling, records chasing and the client-status agent quoted separately - INFERENCE
suggested_pricing.reasoning: INFERENCE, reasoned against published competitor prices and the audit's own impact range. (a) Competitor anchor: AI Esquire charges $497/mo for about 100 calls and $997/mo for 100-300 calls; Smith.ai charges $500/mo for 300 AI-handled calls; Ruby charges $1,725/mo for 500 live minutes, which for 1,800 minutes of after-hours volume would run to thousands per month. $650/mo therefore sits between AI Esquire's Starter and Growth tiers and far below a live answering service at this volume, while our running cost is roughly $115-$140/mo, so gross margin is about 80%. (b) Value anchor: the audit puts recoverable staff time at about $2,700-$18,100 a year, i.e. $225-$1,508 a month, so $650/mo only pays back inside the middle-to-upper half of that range - which is why the pilot is priced to measure capture rate and volume first, and why the engagement should be re-priced once real call counts replace the inference. (c) The setup fee is deliberately below what a custom CRM integration would cost because the build is configuration on an existing platform plus prompts and schema, not new software. (d) No result, client reference or conversion uplift is claimed anywhere in the pitch; the pilot is sold as measurement, and the exit criteria let the firm walk away.

leverage.point: The build is configuration on a per-minute platform, not custom infrastructure: Telnyx charges no monthly platform fee and publishes a complete rate card including transfer, recording and per-part SMS, so a second and third law-firm client can be added by cloning the agent and swapping prompts - the marginal build falls by roughly half on each reuse (inference)

The intake schema, escalation runbook and bilingual prompt set are firm-agnostic assets for plaintiff PI work; every New Jersey PI firm with contingency economics faces the same after-hours problem, so the same core resells into Middlesex, Monmouth and Somerset counties without new engineering

The firm's stack is already integration-ready and already paid for: Lawbrokr publishes webhooks on every plan and Gravity Forms has an official webhooks add-on, so nothing needs ripping out and no new SaaS line item is created

The Spanish requirement is a moat rather than a chore: the whole site is translated and Spanish posts are published, so a genuinely bilingual voice agent is table stakes here and the acoustic/language work done for RAM Law transfers to the next bilingual firm

Local presence is real and cheap: a Milltown founder can sit in the New Brunswick office in under 20 minutes for shadowing, on-call training and quarterly reviews, which national AI-receptionist vendors cannot do

Cost floor: at roughly $0.06/min all-in versus $3.60-$5.00 per live-answering minute implied by Ruby's plan ladder, the same after-hours coverage is delivered at a fraction of the incumbent cost - which is the number that makes a fixed monthly fee easy to defend

edge_vs_competitors: Against national AI receptionists (Smith.ai, AI Esquire, Frontdesk) the edge is specificity and integration: a New Jersey PI intake schema with county-to-office routing, a conservative deadline and public-entity flag, duplicate and conflict screening, and write-back into the firm's own case management - plus a runbook written for RPC 5.3 supervision and signed by a named attorney, which no general receptionist product supplies. Against live answering services (Ruby, Answering Legal, LEX-type vendors) the edge is price at volume (about $0.06/min versus live-minute plans) and structured output rather than a message slip, plus warm transfer for the calls that matter. Against hiring, the edge is 24/7 coverage at roughly one tenth the loaded cost of one secretary. The edge that does NOT exist: brand, references, a 24/7 human floor, SOC 2, a real CRM/product roadmap, and any proof of results - and the firm already runs Lawbrokr, whose higher tiers advertise multilingual AI intake, so the honest position is that we are adding the phone channel and the legal-quality controls, not inventing intake. If Lawbrokr already answers after-hours calls well, this opportunity shrinks and the pitch should move to the records/status opportunities.

risks_compliance.issue: Supervision of an automated nonlawyer assistant: the firm remains responsible for what the agent says to a prospective client
risks_compliance.rule_or_source: NJ Supreme Court preliminary AI guidelines (Jan 24, 2024) state that lawyers' RPC duties are unchanged by AI, and that oversight obligations under RPC 5.1 and RPC 5.3 extend to ensuring the ethical use of AI by nonlawyer staff and outside providers
risks_compliance.mitigation: Written runbook signed by a named supervising attorney; prohibited-phrase list (no advice, no fees, no deadline statements, no acceptance); human approval of every declination; weekly transcript sampling in the supervision file

risks_compliance.issue: Confidentiality of non-public client and caller information flowing through an AI system
risks_compliance.rule_or_source: Same guidelines: RPC 1.6 requires reasonable efforts to prevent inadvertent or unauthorised disclosure, and 'a lawyer is responsible to ensure the security of an AI system before entering any non-public client information'
risks_compliance.mitigation: Single-tenant deployment, zero-retention/no-training settings, per-matter access scoping so one caller's record can never surface in another's answer, encryption at rest, 90-day configurable audio retention, and a written data-handling schedule naming every subprocessor

risks_compliance.issue: Accuracy: a hallucinated deadline, county or legal explanation is a misrepresentation risk, not just a bad UX moment
risks_compliance.rule_or_source: Same guidelines cite RPC 3.1, RPC 4.1(a)(1) and RPC 8.4(c) and state that 'a lawyer has an ethical duty to check and verify all information generated by AI'
risks_compliance.mitigation: Agent never gives legal advice or states a deadline; deadline flags are internal-only and computed conservatively for a human to act on; scripted answers only; blocking verification on any answer that cites a source; zero-tolerance escalation on treatment, deadlines, money and dissatisfaction

risks_compliance.issue: Call recording: the agent records every call, and callers are not always in New Jersey
risks_compliance.rule_or_source: New Jersey is a one-party consent state for telephone recording under N.J.S.A. 2A:156A-3 and -4 (consent of at least one party), unless the recording is made for a criminal or tortious purpose
risks_compliance.mitigation: Keep a spoken disclosure at the top of every call and a recorded consent line on the web form; because a caller may be in a two-party-consent state or the firm may want belt-and-braces, recording disclosure is unconditional rather than relying on the one-party exception

risks_compliance.issue: SMS and any outbound call: consent, opt-out and registration rules apply to messages sent by software
risks_compliance.rule_or_source: 47 CFR 64.1200 requires prior express consent for autodialed/prerecorded calls and texts, and requires that a called party may revoke consent by any reasonable method, honoured within a reasonable time not to exceed ten business days; separately, application-to-person SMS from a US local number requires 10DLC brand and campaign registration
risks_compliance.mitigation: Only message people who called the firm or submitted the form (transactional confirmation, not marketing); capture the consent language on the form; honour STOP and any reasonable revocation across all channels; register brand and campaign before go-live; no marketing sequences from this system at all

risks_compliance.issue: Health information in injury narratives (treatment, diagnoses, providers)
risks_compliance.rule_or_source: Under 45 CFR 160.103 a 'covered entity' is a health plan, a health care clearinghouse or a health care provider transmitting health information electronically - a plaintiff law firm is none of these, so HIPAA does not directly govern it (inference from the definition); obligations arrive contractually through providers and through the firm's own confidentiality duty
risks_compliance.mitigation: Treat all treatment detail as confidential regardless of HIPAA status: choose subprocessors that will sign a BAA (Deepgram states BAA availability for Enterprise), minimise PHI in prompts, redact provider identifiers from logs where not needed

risks_compliance.issue: Deadline automation: the agent's most dangerous feature is the one that looks most useful
risks_compliance.rule_or_source: N.J.S.A. 2A:14-2 sets a two-year limitation for personal-injury actions; claims against public entities run through the Tort Claims Act with a separate notice-of-claim process (the exact notice period could not be confirmed from an opened primary source in this session)
risks_compliance.mitigation: Deadline flags are internal, advisory and conservative only; no date is ever given to a caller; every flag shows its arithmetic and requires a human to accept it; the firm's docketing system remains the system of record

risks_compliance.issue: Unauthorised practice of law and accidental creation of an attorney-client relationship by a nonlawyer agent
risks_compliance.rule_or_source: The NJ guidelines' oversight section and RPC 5.3 put responsibility for nonlawyer and outside-provider conduct on the firm; the specific text of RPC 5.5 could not be opened during this session
risks_compliance.mitigation: Agent states that it is an intake assistant and not a lawyer, never says 'we will represent you', routes any request for legal advice to a person, and every engagement decision is made by a lawyer; scripts reviewed by counsel before go-live

risks_compliance.issue: Vendor claims about results and the temptation to repeat them in the pitch
risks_compliance.rule_or_source: Vendor case studies (e.g. '52% conversion rate') are marketing claims, not measurements; the analyst found no peer-reviewed field study of law-firm intake savings
risks_compliance.mitigation: Pitch and report only the firm's own measured baseline and after numbers; quote no competitor results and no conversion uplift; keep the audit's labour-hour range labelled as an estimate

feasibility.weeks_to_pilot: 7-8 weeks from signed agreement to live after-hours pilot (3-4 weeks build, 3-4 weeks live)
feasibility.reasoning: Technical 4/5: every layer of the design has a published, priced API - Telnyx voice and messaging, Gravity Forms webhooks, Lawbrokr webhooks, Deepgram multilingual STT - and the after-hours window is a low-blast-radius place to start because no daytime call and no acceptance decision is touched. It is not 5/5 because the firm's phone system and case management system are both unknown, and write-back into the case file is the one integration that could turn into a multi-week unblockable dependency. Commercial 3/5: the firm has clear ability to pay (three offices, 11 certified trial attorneys, $170M+ recovered, a COO and a marketing director, heavy paid acquisition), and the price sits comfortably inside published competitor ranges - but three things are unproven and must be settled in discovery: whether after-hours calls are already answered acceptably by an incumbent vendor, whether the volume is at the upper end of the assumed 150-400 inquiries a month (at the low end the monthly fee exceeds the measured savings), and whether Lawbrokr's own AI intake already covers part of this. Conditions for a Go: discovery confirms a real after-hours capture or re-entry gap; the firm names a supervising attorney and adopts the runbook; case management write-back is achievable via API or clean export; and a bilingual reviewer signs off the Spanish flow. If discovery shows Lawbrokr or an answering service already capturing after-hours calls well, switch the pitch to the records/bill chase or the client-status agent rather than forcing this one.

discovery_questions: What happens today to a call that comes in at 9pm on a Tuesday or 2pm on a Sunday - who answers, what do they record, and where does that record go?
Which vendor or service handles after hours now, what does it cost per month, and what is in the contract (term, per-minute rate, cancellation)?
On an average month, how many inbound calls and form submissions do you get, and what share arrive outside 8am-8pm?
From your CallRail reports, what percentage of after-hours calls are answered versus abandoned or sent to voicemail?
Which case management system do you use, does it have an API or export, and who administers it?
What phone system runs the three offices, and can calls be forwarded by time-of-day and by hunt group?
Which intake questions are mandatory for your screening, and which answers cause you to decline a matter outright?
Who is on the after-hours on-call rotation for injuries, and how are they reached today?
Does Lawbrokr currently answer anything live, or is it website intake only?
Is there a written intake script or training document, and may we see it?
Which attorney will supervise this and sign the runbook, and what phrases do you never want said to a caller?
What bilingual capacity exists on staff today, and how do you currently handle a Spanish-only caller after hours?
What would make you switch this off after four weeks - what does failure look like to you?
Do you want callbacks booked directly into staff calendars, or queued to the front desk each morning?
caveats: No client, result or conversion claim is made anywhere in this plan; the founder has no law-firm clients and should say so.

All volumes, minutes and cost arithmetic above the published rate cards are inferences (150-400 inquiries/month, 25-40% after hours, ~6 minutes per call, 1,800 minutes/month); they must be replaced with the firm's CallRail data in week 1.

The audit's $2,700-$18,100/year impact figure is a labour-hour floor at NJ median wages, not a revenue or settlement figure, and it understates the loaded cost of an hour because benefits are applied at a rough 1.25 multiplier.

Vendor pages change; every price here was read on 2026-11-12 and should be re-checked before it appears in a proposal. AI Esquire and Frontdesk quotes are retail list prices with self-serve checkout; Lawbrokr, Answering Legal and the case management system are quote-based.

The single biggest unknown is whether after-hours calls are already handled acceptably. If an incumbent answering service is doing well, the honest pitch changes to records/bill chasing or client status.

Lawbrokr is already installed and its higher tiers advertise multilingual AI intake, so part of this opportunity may already be paid for and unused; discovery must check what tier the firm is on and what the widget currently does.
data_gaps: CallRail's own pricing page is JavaScript-rendered and could not be opened, and developers.callrail.com did not resolve, so its API/webhook documentation and per-plan price could not be confirmed - the design therefore avoids depending on it.
The firm's phone system, case management, document management and billing software are unknown; nothing on the site names them.
Who answers after-hours calls today is unknown (answering service, vendor, or staff rotation).
Gravity Forms licence tier and add-on price are not published on the add-on page; the firm's existing licence tier is unknown.
Lawbrokr's plan prices are not published (billed annually, quoted by sales), so no comparison figure could be recorded for the product the firm already runs.
LEX Reception's own pricing page returned HTTP 404 during research, so it is not included as a priced competitor.

The full text of the NJ Rules of Professional Conduct (njcourts.gov rpc.pdf) returned HTTP 404; RPC 5.1, 5.3, 1.6, 3.1, 4.1 and 8.4 are therefore cited through the Supreme Court's AI guidelines notice, and RPC 5.5 (unauthorised practice) could not be confirmed from a primary text.
The Tort Claims Act notice-of-claim period (commonly 90 days) could not be confirmed from an opened primary source; the NJ Treasury claim page describes the process but not the deadline.
The status of any comprehensive New Jersey consumer privacy statute was not confirmed in this session, and no NJ-specific AI or automated-decision law applicable to a law firm's intake was located.
HIPAA's non-application to a plaintiff law firm is an inference from the 45 CFR 160.103 definition, not a regulator's statement about law firms.
No independent measure of the firm's intake volume, after-hours call volume, conversion rate or current answering-service cost exists publicly; the firm publishes none.
No peer-reviewed study quantifying law-firm intake automation savings was located, so no benchmark uplift is claimed.
